title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam in which AI-generated deepfake images, videos, and fabricated text were used to create a fake news article depicting a conversation between two real, named public figures that never took place. The failure did not originate inside a legitimate AI deployment, it is a case of AI tools being used by external actors to produce fraudulent content. The point of vulnerability is the distribution layer, the platforms and advertising networks that carried the fake article to potential investors without detecting or removing it.

The scale described by ASIC, tens of thousands of scams removed in a single year with a reported large percentage increase, indicates that the volume of such content has outpaced platform moderation. Catching this kind of fraud requires verifying whether named individuals actually participated in the content attributed to them, a check that automated content moderation does not reliably perform and that most consumers have no straightforward way to carry out themselves.

What is not established is whether any specific platform acted with knowledge of the fraudulent content, or whether the unlicensed platform Boulder Sparhaven has been formally found liable for any losses.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featured a fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article depicted an argument that never occurred. This type of scam is becoming increasingly common, with artificial intelligence making fraudulent content more convincing and difficult to detect. ASIC research reveals these schemes are growing more sophisticated, using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to promote illegitimate investments.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, including 5,476 phishing scams and 7,051 fake investment platforms. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, and finance presenter Alan Kohler are among the most commonly impersonated Australians, along with wealthy figures like Gina Rinehart and Dick Smith. Scammers build elaborate fake websites, news articles, and advertisements to deceive consumers. ASIC recommends verifying Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing, while Kohler argues platforms distributing such content should face heavy fines.
